newsitem.title: USA: USW struggle at Bridgestone not yet done.
newsitem.headline: USW struggle at Bridgestone not yet done.

text.p: United Steelworkers union officials, after reaching a tentative agreement with Bridgestone Corp's Bridgestone/Firestone Inc that they labeled a victory, on Wednesday backed off from saying their long and bitter labor dispute with the company was over.
"There are still a lot of issues to be worked out," USW President George Becker said at a news conference. "We hope this is the end of a long struggle with the company."
Nashville-based Bridgestone/Firestone is the U.S. arm of Japanese tire maker Bridgestone Corp.
The union has been locked in a bitter dispute with the company that began with a July 1994 strike launched by the former United Rubber Workers union.
The company hired replacement workers in January 1995. The following May, the union offered an unconditional return to work, ending the strike.
Two months later, the rubber workers merged with the steelworkers and launched a "corporate campaign" against the company to boycott its products among car dealers, tire distributors and consumers.
Workers were called back periodically over several months but were working under proposals offered by the company before the strike began.
The tentative agreement was reached early Monday after several days of round-the-clock negotiations. It covers more than 6,000 workers at five tire plants, mostly in the Midwest.
The agreement is subject to a ratification vote by workers, tentatively scheduled for mid December. Becker said prior to that vote, local issues at each plant must be worked out.

The tentative pact includes a wage increase of 40 cents an hour; a $750 signing bonus; an increase in holidays; health program improvements and elimination of premiums; supplemental bonuses for strikers who returned to work; and a provision that requires a buyer of a company plant to negotiate a contract with the union.
"This was perhaps one of the most difficult and significant struggles the labor movement has ever faced," Becker said.

John Sellers, executive vice president of the USW's rubber division, said the union was unable to negotiate job security provisions in the new agreement. "We didn't address that to our satisfaction," he said.

Steelworkers at U.S. steel producers have contracts that contain no-layoff provisions. Sellers said the new pact contains supplemental unemployment benefits. "We have always considered (those benefits) a deterrent to layoffs," he said.
Sellers said there are about 250-300 replacement workers still in the tire plants affected by the strike.
